name: Malick Sidibé
milestone_by_age_26: Began working as an independent professional photographer in Bamako in 1957 after his mentor Gérard Guillat closed his studio, documenting the city's youth culture and nightlife.
early_history_summary: Born to a Fulani peasant family in rural Soloba, Mali, Sidibé herded sheep as a child and started school late. His drawing talent won him a place at the École des Artisans Soudanais in Bamako in 1952. In 1955, society photographer Gérard Guillat hired him as an apprentice, where Sidibé learned photography and eventually took on his own clients. When Guillat closed his studio in 1957, Sidibé began independently photographing Bamako nightlife and social events.
family_context_summary: Born to a Fulani peasant farming family in the village of Soloba, 300 km from Bamako; his father was a stock breeder, farmer, and skilled hunter who wanted Malick to attend school but died before he could arrange it.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Father was a farmer and hunter with no known connection to photography or the arts.
primary_early_advantage_tags: mentor apprenticeship, art school, cultural frontier, rural-to-urban
evidence_summary: Sidibé rose from a rural peasant background to become a photographer through a fortuitous apprenticeship with Gérard Guillat, who provided sustained mentorship and access to camera equipment in 1950s Mali. His natural drawing talent was noticed early, earning him a place at a Bamako art school. The post-independence cultural flowering of Bamako in the early 1960s provided a structural wave that amplified his work. He was blind in one eye from a childhood accident, adding an adversity dimension to his achievement.
starting_point: Born to a Fulani peasant farming family in the village of Soloba, Mali; father was a stock breeder and hunter who died before arranging schooling.
current_position: Died on 14 April 2016 in Bamako at age 80; final role: renowned photographer operating Studio Malick in Bamako, recipient of the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement (2007) and Hasselblad Award (2003).

trajectory.event: Won a place at the École des Artisans Soudanais in Bamako on the strength of his drawing talent.
Hired as an apprentice by society photographer Gérard Guillat, learning photography and taking on his own clients.
Began working as an independent photographer after Guillat closed his studio, documenting Bamako nightlife and youth culture.
Opened his own photography studio, Studio Malick, in the Bagadadji neighborhood of Bamako.
Had his first exhibition outside Mali, launching his international art career.
Received the prestigious Hasselblad Award for photography.
Awarded the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale, the first photographer and first African so honored.
Died on 14 April 2016 in Bamako from complications of diabetes.

name: Richard Krajicek
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1996 Wimbledon men's singles title, becoming the first Dutch man to win a Grand Slam singles title, at age 25.
early_history_summary: Born in Rotterdam to Czech immigrant parents, Krajicek began playing tennis at age four under his father Petr's guidance. He won the Dutch under-12 and under-14 national championships twice each. He turned professional in 1989 at age 17 and won his first ATP singles title in Hong Kong in 1991 at age 19. He reached the Australian Open semifinals in 1992 and the French Open semifinals in 1993, establishing himself as a top player before his Wimbledon breakthrough.
family_context_summary: Born in Rotterdam to Czech immigrant parents; his father Petr put a tennis racket in his hand at age four and insisted on practice, providing early domain exposure and motivation.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Dutch tennis federation, father coaching, junior championships, elite coaching
evidence_summary: Krajicek benefited from his father's early introduction to tennis at age four and the Dutch Tennis Federation's elite coaching pipeline under Stanley Franker, who provided sustained, structured training. He dominated Dutch junior tennis, winning national championships at under-12 and under-14 levels. The Federation's systematic approach—satellite and challenger circuits, specialized coaches like Rohan Goetzke—concentrated opportunity for top juniors. His Czech immigrant family provided a sport-oriented household, though not exceptional wealth.
starting_point: Born in Rotterdam to Czech immigrant parents; father Petr introduced him to tennis at age four and insisted on daily practice, creating a sport-focused household.
current_position: Retired from professional tennis in 2003; founder of the Krajicek Foundation which builds tennis courts in underprivileged Dutch neighborhoods; career-high ranking world No. 4; resides in the Netherlands.

trajectory.event: Turned professional tennis player, ranked 392nd in the world.
Won his first ATP top-level singles title in Hong Kong.
Reached the Australian Open singles semifinals, a Grand Slam breakthrough.
Won the Wimbledon men's singles title, defeating Pete Sampras in the quarterfinals and MaliVai Washington in the final.
Achieved career-high singles ranking of world No. 4.
Retired from the professional tennis tour with 17 singles titles and 3 doubles titles.

name: İbrahim Tatlıses
milestone_by_age_26: Released the smash-hit album 'Ayağında Kundura' in 1977 at age 25, which propelled him to national fame across Turkey.
early_history_summary: Born in a cave in Urfa, Turkey to an Arab father and Kurdish mother, Tatlıses grew up in extreme poverty, lost his father in childhood, and never attended school. He began amateur cassette recordings at age 15, singing at weddings and restaurants in Urfa and nearby cities. He performed at music halls in Adana and then Ankara, where his powerful voice built a local following. A producer discovered him in 1976, leading to his breakthrough album the following year.
family_context_summary: Born in extreme poverty in Urfa to an Arab father (who was in jail when İbrahim was born) and a Kurdish mother; he was the eldest of seven children, grew up in a cave-like dwelling, lost his father during childhood, and never attended school.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No evidence of parental involvement in music or entertainment.
primary_early_advantage_tags: extreme poverty, self-taught, remarkable voice, wedding performances
evidence_summary: Tatlıses rose from one of the most impoverished backgrounds imaginable—born in a cave, illiterate, fatherless—to become Turkey's most famous Arabesk singer through sheer vocal talent and relentless performing at weddings and restaurants from age 15. No family resources, formal training, or institutional pipeline supported him. His discovery by a producer in 1976 was the result of years of grassroots performing. His adversity was extreme and directly catalyzed his drive to escape poverty through music.
starting_point: Born in extreme poverty in a cave in Urfa, Turkey to an Arab father (imprisoned at birth) and Kurdish mother; eldest of seven children, illiterate, fatherless from childhood.
current_position: Still active as a singer and cultural icon in Turkey; survived a 2011 assassination attempt (shot in the head); known as 'İmparator' (Emperor) of Turkish music with 42 albums recorded from 1970 to 2014.

trajectory.event: Released his first amateur tape 'Kara Kız/Beni Yakma Gel Güzelim' and began performing at weddings and restaurants.
Released the smash-hit album 'Ayağında Kundura,' propelling him to national fame across Turkey.
Embarked on his film career with 'Ayağında Kundura-Ceylan,' beginning decades of acting.
Became host of the highly popular television programme 'İbo Show,' cementing his cultural dominance.
Survived an assassination attempt, being shot in the head, and continued his career after recovery.

name: Damir Skomina

evidence_summary: Skomina's refereeing career began at 16, and he reached the Slovenian first division by 23, but all material international milestones (FIFA listing, Champions League, European Championship, World Cup, Champions League final) occurred after age 26. name: Martin Evans
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Evans earned his BA in Biochemistry from Cambridge in 1963 and was pursuing his PhD at University College London (awarded 1969) during his mid-twenties. His Nobel-winning discovery of embryonic stem cells came in 1981 at age 40.
early_history_summary: Evans studied at a prep school where a teacher inspired his interest in biology, then won a major scholarship to Christ's College, Cambridge, where he studied biochemistry. After graduating in 1963, he began PhD research at University College London on genetic control of vertebrate development. His seminal work isolating embryonic stem cells did not come until 1981.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources in detail; attended prep school suggesting a middle-class or affluent background.
evidence_summary: Evans had strong educational foundations—Cambridge scholarship, excellent teaching—but his material scientific milestone (isolating embryonic stem cells) came at age 40 in 1981. By age 26 he was a PhD student with no independently verifiable material milestone.

name: Finn Bálor
milestone_by_age_26: Won the IWGP Junior Heavyweight Tag Team Championship with Minoru in January 2008 at NJPW, one of the world's premier wrestling promotions, at age 26.
early_history_summary: Born Fergal Devitt in Bray, County Wicklow, Ireland, he was a wrestling fan from childhood. He trained at NWA UK Hammerlock and debuted on 23 November 2001 at age 20. He quickly won the NWA British Commonwealth Heavyweight Championship and co-founded NWA Ireland in 2002. He signed with New Japan Pro-Wrestling in 2006 and debuted there as Prince Devitt, joining the CTU faction and forming a tag team with Minoru that won the IWGP Junior Heavyweight Tag Team Championship in January 2008.
family_context_summary: Born in Bray, County Wicklow, Ireland; grew up as a wrestling fan watching WWF. Limited family background detail available in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No evidence of family involvement in wrestling or athletics.
primary_early_advantage_tags: NWA training, early debut, NJPW signing, tag team championship
evidence_summary: Devitt built his wrestling career through grassroots training at NWA UK Hammerlock and early independent circuit work, founding his own promotion (NWA Ireland) at 21. His signing with NJPW in 2006 at age 25 was a career-defining break, giving him access to one of the world's elite wrestling platforms. His tag team championship win at 26 was the product of sustained reps and progressive skill development rather than inherited advantage.
starting_point: Born in Bray, County Wicklow, Ireland; grew up as a passionate wrestling fan in a working-class Irish town with no documented family connection to the sport.
current_position: Signed to WWE on the SmackDown brand as Finn Bálor; former WWE Universal Champion and NXT Champion; member of The Judgment Day faction; resides in the United States.

trajectory.event: Made his professional wrestling debut on 23 November after training at NWA UK Hammerlock.
Co-founded NWA Ireland, his own wrestling promotion, and won the NWA British Commonwealth Heavyweight Championship.
Signed with New Japan Pro-Wrestling (NJPW) and debuted as Prince Devitt.

Signed with WWE and debuted in NXT, beginning his Finn Bálor persona.
Became the inaugural WWE Universal Champion at SummerSlam.

name: Andreas Brehme
milestone_by_age_26: Earned his first cap for the West Germany national team in 1984 at age 24 and was named in the team of the tournament at the 1984 European Championship, while established as a starting left-back for 1. FC Kaiserslautern in the Bundesliga.
early_history_summary: Born in Hamburg, Brehme started his football career at HSV Barmbek-Uhlenhorst, his father Bernd's club, joining the youth system at age 5 in 1965. He made his senior debut for the club in 1978 at age 18, moved to 1. FC Saarbrücken in 1980, and joined Bundesliga side 1. FC Kaiserslautern in 1981 at age 21, where he became a key player. He earned his first international cap for West Germany in 1984 and was named in the Euro 1984 team of the tournament.
primary_leverage_engine: Early specialization and family domain exposure
family_context_summary: Born in Hamburg, the son of Bernd Brehme, a footballer who played for HSV Barmbek-Uhlenhorst; Andreas played his early football for his father's lower-league side, providing direct domain exposure from childhood.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Bernd Brehme was a footballer at HSV Barmbek-Uhlenhorst, providing Andreas with early coaching, club access, and football culture immersion from age 5.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father footballer, youth system, Bundesliga, ambidextrous talent
evidence_summary: Brehme grew up in a football household—his father Bernd was a footballer and coach at HSV Barmbek-Uhlenhorst, where Andreas began playing at age 5. This family-domain apprenticeship gave him 13 years in the youth system before his senior debut at 18. His rare ambidextrous ability set him apart technically. The German football pipeline provided a clear path from lower leagues to the Bundesliga and national team, which he navigated rapidly, reaching international level by 24.
starting_point: Born in Hamburg, son of Bernd Brehme, a footballer at local club HSV Barmbek-Uhlenhorst; grew up immersed in football culture from early childhood.
current_position: Died on 20 February 2024 in Munich at age 63 from a heart attack; final role: former football coach, remembered as a World Cup-winning left-back for Germany.

trajectory.event: Made his senior football debut for HSV Barmbek-Uhlenhorst in the Amateur-Oberliga Nord.
Joined 1. FC Kaiserslautern in the Bundesliga, establishing himself as a top-division professional.
Earned his first cap for West Germany and was named in the team of the tournament at Euro 1984.
Played in the FIFA World Cup final for West Germany and joined Bayern Munich for a record transfer fee.
Won the Serie A title with Inter Milan and was named Italian Footballer of the Year.
Scored the winning penalty in the FIFA World Cup final for Germany against Argentina.
Won the Bundesliga title with 1. FC Kaiserslautern in his final playing season.
Died of a heart attack on 20 February 2024 in Munich.

name: Satish Kumar
milestone_by_age_26: Initiated an 8,000-mile peace pilgrimage on foot from New Delhi to Moscow, Paris, London, and Washington D.C. in June 1962 at age 25–26, carrying no money, to advocate for nuclear disarmament.
early_history_summary: Born in Sri Dungargarh, Rajasthan, India, Kumar's father died when he was four. At age nine, inspired by Jain monks, he renounced the world and became a wandering Jain monk. At 18, after reading Gandhi, he left the monastic order and joined Vinoba Bhave's land reform movement. Inspired by Bertrand Russell's anti-nuclear activism, he and companion E.P. Menon embarked on a two-and-a-half-year peace walk to the capitals of the four nuclear-armed nations in June 1962.
family_context_summary: Born in Sri Dungargarh, Rajasthan; his father died when he was four, leaving his mother to raise eight children. The family was of modest peasant background with deep spiritual inclinations.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No evidence of parental involvement in activism or public life; mother was described as religious with 'peasant wisdom.'
primary_early_advantage_tags: Jain monasticism, Gandhi legacy, Vinoba Bhave mentorship, nuclear disarmament movement
evidence_summary: Kumar's extraordinary early life—fatherless at four, a Jain monk by nine, then a Gandhian activist by 18—gave him deep spiritual discipline and a network through Vinoba Bhave's movement. The nuclear disarmament movement of the early 1960s provided a structural wave. His peace walk was a feat of physical and moral endurance shaped by monastic training and adversity, not by family resources or institutional pipelines. His companion E.P. Menon provided a complementary partnership.
starting_point: Born in Sri Dungargarh, Rajasthan, India to a modest peasant family; father died when he was four, leaving his mother to raise eight children.
current_position: Founder and Director of Programmes of Schumacher College; Editor Emeritus of Resurgence & Ecologist magazine; living in England at age 88, continuing to speak and write on ecology and peace.

trajectory.event: Renounced the world and became a wandering Jain monk, beginning years of ascetic spiritual training.
Left the Jain monastic order after reading Gandhi and joined Vinoba Bhave's land reform movement.
Initiated an 8,000-mile peace pilgrimage on foot from India to the four nuclear capitals, carrying no money.
Co-founded the London School of Non-Violence in tribute to Mahatma Gandhi's centenary.
Became editor of Resurgence magazine, a role he would hold for over 40 years.
Founded Schumacher College, an international center for ecological studies in Devon, England.

name: Melvin Manhoef

name: Zoran Slavnić
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Yugoslav National Championship with Crvena zvezda in 1969 at age 20, followed by a second national championship in 1972, three national cups, and a EuroBasket gold medal with Yugoslavia in 1973 at age 24.
early_history_summary: Born in Belgrade, Slavnić joined the Crvena zvezda basketball system as a youth, developing under coaches Ranko Žeravica and Mirko Novosel. He made his senior debut for Crvena zvezda in 1967 at age 18 and won his first Yugoslav National Championship in 1969 at age 20. He became one of the best point guards in European basketball, winning multiple national titles and international medals with Yugoslavia by his mid-twenties.
family_context_summary: Born in Belgrade, PR Serbia, FPR Yugoslavia. Limited family background documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Crvena zvezda, Yugoslav basketball, elite coaching, national team
evidence_summary: Slavnić developed within the Crvena zvezda basketball system in Belgrade, one of the top clubs in the dominant Yugoslav basketball ecosystem. Coaches Ranko Žeravica and Mirko Novosel provided high-quality training, though Žeravica initially considered him undisciplined. The Yugoslav national team pipeline concentrated elite talent and provided a path to international medals. By his mid-twenties, Slavnić had won multiple national championships and a EuroBasket gold, benefiting from being immersed in one of the world's strongest basketball development systems.
starting_point: Born in Belgrade, Yugoslavia; family background not documented in reviewed sources, but grew up in one of Europe's premier basketball cities.
current_position: Retired from basketball; last known coaching role with the Serbia national team in 2007; named one of FIBA's 50 Greatest Players in 1991 and inducted into the FIBA Hall of Fame in 2013; living in Belgrade at age 76.

trajectory.event: Made his senior debut for Crvena zvezda Belgrade, beginning a 10-season career with the club.
Won the Yugoslav National Championship with Crvena zvezda, his first national title.
Won his second Yugoslav National Championship with Crvena zvezda.
Won EuroBasket gold with Yugoslavia in Barcelona, his first major international medal.
Won the FIBA Saporta Cup with Crvena zvezda and earned World Championship silver with Yugoslavia.
Won the FIBA World Championship gold medal with Yugoslavia in Manila.
Won Olympic gold with Yugoslavia at the Moscow Olympics.
Inducted into the FIBA Hall of Fame as a player.

name: Susumu Tonegawa
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Tonegawa graduated from the University of Kyoto in 1963 and was a PhD student at UC San Diego from 1963 to 1968. His Nobel-winning discovery on antibody diversity gene rearrangement was published in 1976 at age 37.
early_history_summary: Born in Nagoya, Japan, Tonegawa was educated at Hibiya High School in Tokyo and entered the University of Kyoto in 1959 to study chemistry, graduating in 1963. He moved to UC San Diego for graduate study in molecular biology under Masaki Hayashi, receiving his PhD in 1968. His landmark immunology work at the Basel Institute for Immunology came in the 1970s.
family_context_summary: Born in Nagoya, Japan, the second of four children. Educated at Hibiya High School in Tokyo, suggesting a family that valued education. Limited family background documented.
evidence_summary: Tonegawa had strong educational foundations—University of Kyoto, then UC San Diego for his PhD—but his material scientific milestone (discovering the genetic principle for antibody diversity) came at age 37 in 1976. By age 26 he was a PhD student with no independently verifiable material milestone.

name: Dmitry Muserskiy
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 2012 Olympic gold medal with the Russian national team at the London Olympics at age 24, scoring a match-high 31 points in the final against Brazil after being switched to the opposite position.
early_history_summary: Born in Makiivka, Ukraine, Soviet Union, Muserskiy began playing volleyball at age 8 under coach Boris Osnach, encouraged by a PE teacher who knew his mother had played volleyball professionally. He joined VBK Kharkiv's youth system and moved to Belogorie Belgorod in Russia in 2005 at age 17. He gained Russian citizenship in 2006 and debuted for the Russian national team in 2010 at age 22, winning the FIVB World League and World Cup in 2011 before his Olympic triumph in 2012.
family_context_summary: Born in Makiivka, Ukraine; his mother played volleyball professionally and his father was a good swimmer, providing a sport-oriented family background. A PE teacher who had taught his parents directed him to volleyball at age 8.
parent_family_domain_summary: Mother played volleyball professionally and father was a strong swimmer; the family's athletic background was known to the PE teacher who directed Dmitry to volleyball, providing early domain exposure.
primary_early_advantage_tags: exceptional height (2.18m), volleyball mother, elite club pipeline, Olympic gold
evidence_summary: Muserskiy's extraordinary physical stature (2.18m / 7'2") was the defining advantage that changed institutional response to him from childhood. His mother's professional volleyball background provided domain proximity, and the PE teacher who knew the family directed him to the sport at age 8. The pipeline from VBK Kharkiv to Belogorie Belgorod—one of Russia's elite volleyball clubs—concentrated his development. By 24, he was an Olympic champion, scoring a record 31 points in the final.
starting_point: Born in Makiivka, Ukraine, Soviet Union to an athletic family; mother played volleyball professionally and father was a strong swimmer, providing a sport-oriented household.
current_position: Playing for the Suntory Sunbirds in Japan's V.League since 2018; 2012 Olympic champion and 2013 European champion with Russia; among the world's tallest professional athletes at 2.18m.

trajectory.event: Began playing volleyball under coach Boris Osnach in Makiivka, directed to the sport by a PE teacher who knew his athletic family.
Joined Belogorie Belgorod, one of Russia's elite volleyball clubs, beginning his professional career.

Moved to Japan to play for the Suntory Sunbirds, helping end their 14-year title drought.
